blocks.intro: More than half of Algonquin homes were built in the 1990s and 2000s, and their leaks tend to start in a few places.

items.h3: Supply Lines at the End of Their Life
items.body: Braided lines under sinks and toilets and washer hoses installed with the house are now 17 years old or more.
Two-story homes put bathrooms over living space. A slow leak shows up as a ceiling stain below.
A cracked ice maker line or a weeping water heater can soak a finished space before you notice.
Pipes over garages and in exterior walls can split in a cold snap. See [burst pipe repair](/algonquin/burst-pipe-repair).

items.q: How can I tell if I have a leak?
items.preview: Turn off all water and watch the meter.
items.answer: Turn off every fixture and appliance and watch your water meter. If it moves, there's a leak.

items.q: Should I replace old supply lines before they leak?
items.preview: If they're original to a 1990s or 2000s home, yes.
items.answer: Yes, if they're original. Braided supply lines and washer hoses don't last forever, and replacing them is inexpensive compared to a flooded floor.

items.q: Can you find a leak without opening walls?
items.answer: Usually. We use moisture meters and listening equipment to find the spot before opening a small area.

items.q: Is a ceiling stain always a leak?
items.preview: Usually. Get it checked before it spreads.
items.answer: Usually, especially under a bathroom. It could also be condensation or a roof leak. We'll find the source.

items.q: What does leak repair cost in Algonquin?
items.preview: It depends on the leak and access. The price comes first.
items.answer: It depends on where the leak is, the pipe and how we reach it. We quote a flat rate before we start.
